item.title: What to Do When You’re Caught in the Middle of a Breakup
item.description:
Divorce

What to Do When You’re Caught in the Middle of a Breakup

Navigating someone else's breakup is about betrayal, loyalty, and varying truths.

Posted August 15, 2026

Key points
  • When someone close to you is getting divorced or in a breakup, it is easy to feel pressure to take sides.
  • Help both sides understand your feelings and keep clear boundaries between the relationships.
  • The best you can do is be honest, sensitive, and emotionally generous.
Source: jhenning/Pixabay

Divorces and breakups are tough not only for the two people involved but also for their friends and families. Suddenly, you’re feeling stuck in the middle of a collapsing relationship—of your parents, children, siblings, or best friend—over which you have no control. But it is not just them you are concerned about; it is also the “others”—your brother-in-law or son-in-law, or your friend’s partner—with whom you also have a relationship.

And so, you can feel pressure to take sides: Your sister doesn’t understand why you’re not as angry with your brother-in-law as she is, even though, in her mind, you’ve seen how critical or explosive he can be; your daughter expects you to cut off your son-in-law and show loyalty to her; your best friend sees any contact with her ex as somehow watering down your support for her. But it’s not that simple: Your brother-in-law has always been kind and generous to you; you’re hesitant to cut off your son-in-law because you worry about the impact it may have on your grandkids; you’ve known the former partner longer than your best friend and don’t want to lose that relationship.

How do you navigate what feels so awkward? Here are some suggestions:

If you agree to step back from the secondary relationship, still try to get closure.

If you decide it is important to step up, support your sister, and pull back from your brother-in-law, make an effort to find closure with him. Do your best to help them understand your feelings and show appreciation for the positives in your past relationship.

If you decide it’s important to you to keep the relationship with the other person, help them understand why.

If, for example, you do feel, for your grandkids' sake, that it is important to stay connected in some way with your son-in-law, albeit more minimally, help your daughter understand why. People see your behavior, not your intentions. Do your best to explain them.

If you keep both relationships, keep clear boundaries between them.

Don’t rub salt in their wounds by mentioning to your best friend how you saw her ex and how he expressed how much he’s been missing her, or what the grandkids said about their father. Your way out of the middle is to act like you’re not in the middle. Keep your relationships independent.

If your primary person pulls back for whatever reason, keep reaching out.

If your sister, daughter, or best friend stays upset with you, resist the urge to pull back yourself—that only fuels the emotional fire and can easily lead to a standoff that becomes harder to break the longer it continues. Instead, keep reaching out with short texts saying you’re wondering how they’re doing and that you’re happy to talk whenever they’re ready.

And if your primary relationship begins a new relationship, be open-minded and generous.

It’s easy to compare your sister’s new boyfriend to her old one; you may feel concerned that your daughter or best friend is in a dangerous rebound. Resist the urge to compare, be judgmental, or even voice concern unless they ask for your opinion. They need to be able to run their lives as they see fit, just as you do.

The keys here, as in all relationships, are to be honest yet sensitive and to help others understand how you feel and why.

The best you can do is to do the best you can do.

item.title: What Type of People Are Popular at First Sight?
item.description:
Extroversion

What Type of People Are Popular at First Sight?

Perceived assertiveness and sociability are linked with higher popularity.

Posted August 15, 2026

Key points
  • In general, extraverts are perceived as more popular in person and online.
  • Extraverts display more dominant behaviors, impacting perceived popularity.
  • Assertiveness and sociability boost popularity during early stages of a relationship.

During the course of our day when we are in public, we notice certain people more than others. From strangers to social acquaintances, some individuals seem to make a splash every time they enter a room. Confident, calm, and charismatic, they pique our interest, stimulate conversation, and when they are public speakers, they are able to captivate a crowd. Yet when we examine why some of these people are uniquely attractive and memorable, we find that the spell cast may be due to certain behaviors associated with extraversion. Research explains.

Source: Erwin Bosman/Pixabay

Instantly Popular

Martje Buss et al. (2024) explored how extraversion and dominant behavior impact popularity within live and virtual group interaction.[i] They defined popularity as “the extent to which a person is liked by a group of people,” acknowledging a dynamic most of us recognize instinctively. Noting the association between extraversion and popularity, Buss et al. sought to investigate what specific behaviors mediate the link.

Detecting Dominance

In their research, Buss et al. specifically examined how perceived dominant behaviors (nonverbal, paraverbal, verbal, and general cues) impact the relationship between self-rated extraversion and its facets—assertiveness, sociability, and activity, as well as other-rated popularity at a first meeting, often referred to as a setting of “zero-acquaintance.”

In two studies, they analyzed data from face‐to‐face (Study 1) and virtual (Study 2) group interactions where participants performed a task while videotaped, then rated each other on perceived popularity. In both studies, they found that self-reported extraversion was positively associated with other-rated popularity. Specifically, they found that extraversion and the aspects of assertiveness and sociability were consistently linked with higher popularity.

Regarding specific dominant behaviors, Buss et al. found different results in each study. In Study 1, dominant gestures and having an upright posture mediated the association between extraversion and popularity, while in Study 2, all four behavioral cues of dominant behavior (nonverbal, paraverbal, verbal, and general) mediated the association.

Buss et al. concluded that in general, extraverts are perceived as more popular in person and online. They suggest this is because more extraverted people display more dominant behaviors, which impact their perceived popularity, although specific behavioral channels such as verbal, nonverbal, paraverbal, and general may be situation-specific. In addition, Buss et al. note that when examining in detail the different facets of extraversion, assertiveness and sociability appear to be particularly important for perceived popularity during early stages in a relationship.

First Impressions Are Engaging and Enduring

Noting the positive relationship between behavior and popularity explains some of the social dynamics we witness in both public and private interactions. Understanding the power of perception also allows individuals to tailor their presentation to enhance positive qualities, influence, and quality relationships.
